definitions.plain_english: An 'authority' is a special body that the Central Government creates and officially notifies to carry out specific environmental protection tasks on its behalf. This body receives delegated powers — such as issuing binding directions, setting standards, or overseeing pollution control — within the limits set by the Government's order. It acts like an empowered agent of the Central Government for environmental governance purposes.
real_world_examples: The Central Government constituting the Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) under Section 3(3) of the Environment (Protection) Act to regulate extraction of groundwater across India and issue directions to industries and municipalities.

The Central Government establishing the Loss of Ecology (Prevention and Payment of Compensation) Authority for specific regions such as the Aravalli hills to monitor compliance with Supreme Court orders and environmental norms.

The National Coastal Zone Management Authority constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act to supervise implementation of the Coastal Regulation Zone notifications and issue directions to state governments and project proponents.

The Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) constituted for the National Capital Region to direct closure of polluting industries, regulate vehicular emissions, and manage air quality crises in Delhi-NCR.

The Central Government notifying an authority specifically for monitoring and controlling pollution in the Ganga river basin, empowered to issue directions to municipal bodies and industrial units discharging effluents into the river.

An authority empowered to exercise the Central Government's powers under the Act, including issuing binding written directions under Section 5 to persons, officers, or other authorities.
Authorities created for geographically specific or subject-matter-specific environmental mandates, such as regulating coastal zones or managing pollution in a particular river basin.
An authority operating under the supervision and control of the Central Government while independently exercising the delegated powers specified in the constituting order.
Officers appointed under Section 4 who are placed under the direction and control of a Section 3(3) authority, making such authority part of the enforcement chain.
what_it_excludes: State Government bodies or State Pollution Control Boards, which derive their powers from separate legislation such as the Water Act or Air Act, and are not constituted under Section 3(3) of this Act.

The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) or State Pollution Control Boards, as these are statutory bodies constituted under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, not under this Act's Section 3(3).
Individual officers appointed under Section 4 of the Act who, while subject to an authority's direction, are not themselves an 'authority' within the meaning of Section 3(3).
Courts, tribunals such as the National Green Tribunal, or quasi-judicial adjudicatory bodies, which are constituted under separate legislation and exercise judicial rather than executive functions.
Private entities, industry associations, or NGOs, regardless of their environmental role, as only Central Government-constituted bodies qualify as an 'authority' under this provision.

definitions.definition: The Central Government, in the context of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, refers to the Union Government of India, which is vested with the power to take all such measures as it deems necessary or expedient for the purpose of protecting and improving the quality of the environment and preventing, controlling, and abating environmental pollution, and which may issue binding directions, appoint officers, constitute authorities, and make rules for the purposes of this Act.
definitions.plain_english: The Central Government means the Government of India, based in New Delhi, acting through the relevant Union ministries and departments. It is the highest authority under this law, responsible for making rules, setting environmental standards, and giving directions to protect the environment across the entire country. It can also create special bodies or appoint officers to carry out these duties on its behalf.
real_world_examples: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) issuing a notification under the Environment (Protection) Act setting new emission standards for thermal power plants across India.

The Central Government constituting the National Green Tribunal (or a similar authority) and delegating powers under Section 3(3) to oversee environmental compliance in industrial zones in states like Gujarat and Maharashtra.

The Central Government directing, through a written order under Section 5, the closure of a chemical factory in Punjab that is discharging hazardous effluents into the Sutlej river beyond permissible limits.

The Central Government taking cognizance under Section 19 and filing a complaint in a magistrate's court against a company in Jharkhand for violating prescribed environmental standards for air pollution.

The Central Government issuing a notification in the Official Gazette restricting industrial operations within a 10-kilometre radius of the Taj Mahal in Agra to prevent pollution damage to the heritage monument.
The Central Government laying down standards for the handling and disposal of hazardous substances by pharmaceutical companies operating in Hyderabad's pharma cluster under Section 3(2)(g).
what_it_covers: The Union Government of India acting through the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) for all matters under this Act.

Any authority or officer constituted or appointed by the Central Government under Sections 3(3) and 4(1) to whom powers and functions have been expressly delegated for environmental protection purposes.

The exercise of executive power by the Central Government to issue binding written directions under Section 5, including orders for closure, prohibition, or regulation of industries causing environmental pollution.
The Central Government's power to take cognizance of offences and initiate prosecution proceedings under Section 19 of the Act.
The Central Government's power to make rules prescribing standards, procedures, and safeguards for hazardous substances, environmental pollutants, and industrial operations under Section 22.
what_it_excludes: State Governments and their respective environment departments, which are separate governmental entities and operate under their own jurisdiction, though subject to coordination by the Central Government.

Statutory bodies such as the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) or State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs), which are independent authorities created under separate legislation (Water Act, 1974; Air Act, 1981) and are not themselves the Central Government.
Private persons, companies, occupiers, or industry associations, even if they act under a licence or authorisation granted by the Central Government.
Local bodies, municipal corporations, or panchayats, which operate at the local governance level and do not constitute the Central Government for purposes of this Act.
Courts and tribunals, including the National Green Tribunal, which exercise judicial or quasi-judicial functions independently of the Central Government's executive role under this Act.
definitions.why_it_matters: The identification of the Central Government as the competent authority is critical because only the Central Government (or its duly authorised officer or constituted authority) can issue legally binding directions under Section 5, initiate prosecution under Section 19, or make rules with statutory force under Section 22; any direction or action purportedly taken by an entity not constituting the Central Government would lack legal validity and could be challenged as ultra vires. Obligations to comply with directions, standards, and prohibitions under this Act attach only when they are issued or prescribed by the Central Government or its authorised delegates.

definitions.definition: "Company" means any body corporate and includes a firm or other association of individuals.
definitions.plain_english: A 'company' under this law is not limited to formally registered companies. It covers any group or organisation of people working together, including businesses registered as companies, partnerships, and other associations. This broad definition ensures that environmental violations cannot be escaped simply by choosing a particular form of business structure.
real_world_examples: A private limited company registered under the Companies Act, such as a textile dyeing unit in Surat, discharges untreated effluents into a river — the company and its directors in charge can be prosecuted under the Environment Protection Act.

A partnership firm of three individuals operating a chemical manufacturing unit in Ankleshwar, Gujarat, illegally stores hazardous substances without proper safeguards — all partners and the firm itself can be held liable as a 'company' under this Act.

An unregistered association of traders running a waste recycling operation in Delhi's industrial area violates prescribed emission standards — the association qualifies as a 'company' and its members responsible for day-to-day operations face prosecution.

A public sector undertaking (PSU) like a government-owned fertiliser corporation in Uttar Pradesh exceeds prescribed environmental pollutant standards during production — being a body corporate, it falls within the definition of 'company' and its officers can be prosecuted.

A registered cooperative society operating a sugar mill in Maharashtra that discharges untreated effluents into a nearby water body is treated as a 'company' under this Act, making its managing committee members personally liable alongside the society.
what_it_covers: Any body corporate registered under the Companies Act, including private limited companies, public limited companies, and one-person companies operating industrial or commercial activities.
Partnership firms, whether registered or unregistered, engaged in manufacturing, processing, or any industry that may cause environmental pollution.

Any other association of individuals, such as unregistered clubs, cooperative societies, trusts with commercial operations, or trade associations collectively conducting business that falls under the Act.
Public sector undertakings and government-owned corporations that are constituted as bodies corporate and involved in industrial or operational activities.
Limited liability partnerships (LLPs) registered under the LLP Act, which are bodies corporate and therefore squarely within this definition.
what_it_excludes: A sole proprietorship operated by a single individual acting in their own name, as it is neither a body corporate nor a firm or association of individuals.
A natural person acting purely in their individual capacity, who would be prosecuted directly as an individual offender rather than as a 'company'.

A Central or State Government department acting in its sovereign governmental capacity, which is generally not treated as a body corporate or association of individuals for purposes of criminal liability under this provision.
An informal, temporary gathering of individuals with no common business purpose or organisational structure, which would not constitute an 'association of individuals' in the legal sense.
A Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) acting in its capacity as a family unit and not as a registered or constituted business entity, to the extent it lacks the character of a firm or body corporate.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether an entity qualifies as a 'company' under Section 16 determines whether criminal liability for environmental offences can be extended to its responsible officers, directors, managers, and partners — not just the entity itself. If the definition applies, every person in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the company's business at the time of the offence is deemed guilty and can be prosecuted and punished alongside the entity, unless they prove absence of knowledge or exercise of due diligence.

definitions.definition: Connivance, as used in Section 17 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, refers to the tacit or passive agreement, deliberate overlooking, or knowing acquiescence by an officer of a Government Department in the commission of an offence under the Act, without active participation but with full or constructive awareness that the offence is being committed. It implies a voluntary, conscious disregard or silent encouragement of the unlawful act rather than mere inadvertence or ignorance.
definitions.plain_english: Connivance means that an officer knowingly turned a blind eye to an environmental violation happening within their Government Department — they may not have directly ordered or carried out the illegal act, but they were aware of it and deliberately chose to do nothing to stop it. It is more than carelessness but does not require the officer to have actively participated in the wrongdoing. In simple terms, it means silently allowing something illegal to happen when you had the knowledge and power to prevent it.
real_world_examples: A senior officer in a State Pollution Control Department–regulated government factory in Gujarat is informed by a junior engineer that untreated effluents are being discharged into a nearby river, but the senior officer deliberately ignores the reports and takes no corrective action, allowing the illegal discharge to continue — this constitutes connivance.

The Deputy Director of a Central Government–owned thermal power plant in Jharkhand is aware that the plant is emitting particulate matter far beyond prescribed standards but deliberately withholds this information from the Head of the Department and fails to halt operations, thereby conniving in the offence.

A section officer in a Public Works Department in Uttar Pradesh knows that construction debris is being illegally dumped in a protected wetland area by departmental contractors but chooses to look the other way and signs off on completion certificates without raising any objection.

An officer in the Ministry of Defence overseeing a military cantonment in Pune is aware that hazardous waste from the ordnance workshop is being disposed of in violation of prescribed standards under the Environment (Protection) Act but deliberately suppresses internal inspection reports to avoid departmental scrutiny.

A Regional Director of a Central Government–run fertiliser plant in Odisha is repeatedly alerted through internal memos that the plant's ammonia discharge levels exceed environmental limits, but he deliberately delays forwarding complaints to the Head of the Department to protect production targets, thereby conniving in the ongoing violation.
what_it_covers: An officer of a Government Department who is aware of an ongoing environmental violation and deliberately refrains from reporting or stopping it.
A government officer who suppresses internal inspection reports or complaints documenting environmental breaches, thereby allowing the offence to continue unchecked.
A departmental officer who, knowing that prescribed environmental standards are being violated, explicitly or implicitly signals tolerance of the violation to subordinates without formal consent.
A government employee who delays or obstructs mandatory regulatory filings or corrective procedures upon learning of an offence, effectively facilitating its continuation.
what_it_excludes: An officer who genuinely had no knowledge of the offence being committed within their department and therefore could not have acquiesced to it — mere ignorance without constructive knowledge is excluded.
An officer who exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence but failed despite good-faith efforts — diligent but unsuccessful prevention is not connivance.
The Head of the Department, whose liability under Section 17 is governed separately under sub-section (1) and who is specifically excluded from the connivance provision which targets other officers.
Negligent failure to detect an offence where the officer had no reasonable basis to suspect its occurrence — inadvertent omission without awareness falls under neglect, not connivance.
definitions.why_it_matters: If connivance is proved against an officer of a Government Department, that officer is deemed personally guilty of the environmental offence under Section 17(2) and becomes liable to be proceeded against and punished in the same manner as the primary offender, regardless of whether they directly committed the act. This provision pierces the shield of departmental anonymity and ensures that officers who knowingly enable violations cannot escape prosecution by claiming they did not personally carry out the prohibited act.

These labs check whether harmful pollutants are present and at what levels. They are the only labs whose test reports carry legal validity under this law.

Legal text: An environmental laboratory means a laboratory established by the Central Government or recognised by it, by notification in the Official Gazette, under sub-section (1) of section 12 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, for the purpose of carrying out analysis or tests of samples of air, water, soil or other substances to determine the presence, nature and concentration of environmental pollutants.

Examples: The National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), Nagpur, recognised by the Central Government as an environmental laboratory, conducts water quality analysis of samples taken from the Ganga river to check for industrial effluent contamination. | A Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) laboratory in Delhi, notified as an environmental laboratory, analyses air samples collected from industrial zones in Anand Vihar to measure particulate matter and sulphur dioxide levels. | The Environmental Protection Training and Research Institute (EPTRI), Hyderabad, recognised under Section 12, tests soil samples from agricultural land near a chemical plant in Patancheru, Telangana, to detect heavy metal contamination. | A State Government-run institute in Mumbai, duly recognised by the Central Government under Section 12(1), analyses effluent samples collected by authorised officers from a textile dyeing unit in Bhiwandi to determine whether discharge standards are being violated. | The Central Pollution Control Board's laboratory in Kolkata, recognised as an environmental laboratory, tests groundwater samples from areas surrounding a tannery cluster in Kanpur to assess chromium contamination levels for enforcement proceedings.

definitions.definition: "Environmental pollutant" means any solid, liquid or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to environment.
definitions.plain_english: An environmental pollutant is any material — whether solid, liquid, or gas — that exists in an amount high enough to harm or potentially harm the natural environment. The key factor is concentration: even a normally harmless substance can become an environmental pollutant if it is present in excessive quantities. This covers a very wide range of substances across all physical states of matter.
real_world_examples: Untreated industrial effluents discharged by a textile dyeing unit in Tirupur, Tamil Nadu, into the Noyyal River at concentrations toxic to aquatic life, making those effluents environmental pollutants under the Act.

Sulphur dioxide and particulate matter emitted by a thermal power plant in Singrauli, Madhya Pradesh, at levels exceeding prescribed ambient air quality standards, constituting gaseous and solid environmental pollutants.

Fly ash accumulated in unlined ponds near a coal-fired plant in Jharkhand, leaching heavy metals like arsenic and lead into groundwater at injurious concentrations, qualifying fly ash leachate as a liquid environmental pollutant.

Pesticide run-off from agricultural fields in Punjab entering canal water systems at concentrations of organochlorine compounds that are injurious to downstream aquatic ecosystems and human health, making those pesticide residues environmental pollutants.

Noise at excessive decibel levels generated by a stone-crushing unit in an urban area of Maharashtra, which under rules framed pursuant to Section 6, is treated as an environmental pollutant when present at concentrations injurious to the environment and human well-being.
what_it_covers: Liquid effluents such as untreated sewage or chemical wastewater discharged into rivers or groundwater at concentrations injurious to aquatic ecosystems.
Gaseous emissions such as carbon monoxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, or volatile organic compounds released from factories, vehicles, or power plants at harmful concentrations.
Solid substances such as toxic heavy metals, fly ash, plastic waste, or radioactive material deposited in the environment at concentrations that are or tend to be injurious.
Noise, as recognised under rules made under the Act, when present at levels constituting an injurious concentration in the environment.
Substances that are not inherently toxic but become environmental pollutants by virtue of the concentration at which they are present, such as excess nutrients causing eutrophication in water bodies.
what_it_excludes: Substances present in concentrations below any threshold that could be, or tend to be, injurious to the environment — ordinary ambient levels of naturally occurring gases like carbon dioxide within non-harmful ranges do not qualify.
Hazardous substances that are being safely handled, stored, or transported in full compliance with prescribed standards and have not been released into the environment in injurious concentrations.
Biological organisms such as invasive species or pathogens, which are living entities rather than solid, liquid, or gaseous substances as contemplated by the definition.

Energy forms such as heat or radiation in the abstract, unless specifically brought within the scope of rules framed under the Act treating them as environmental pollutants at injurious concentrations.
Substances in transit within a closed, leak-proof industrial system that have not entered or been introduced into the environment in any concentration.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as an environmental pollutant directly determines the applicability of Section 9, which prohibits persons from discharging or emitting such pollutants in excess of prescribed standards, and non-compliance triggers penal consequences under Sections 15–17 of the Act. The definition also governs the Central Government's power to lay down emission and discharge standards under Section 3(2)(d) and the regulatory obligations of occupiers and industries subject to those standards.

definitions.definition: Environmental pollutants refer to any solid, liquid, or gaseous substance present in such concentration as may be, or tend to be, injurious to the environment, as discharged or emitted from various sources including industries, operations, or processes, the standards for which may be prescribed by the Central Government under this Act. The term encompasses all such substances whose emission or discharge into the environment is regulated under the Act, including noise.
definitions.plain_english: Environmental pollutants are harmful substances — whether solid, liquid, or gas — that are released into the air, water, or soil in amounts that can damage the natural environment, human health, or living organisms. This includes things like factory smoke, industrial wastewater, chemical waste dumped into rivers, and even excessive noise. The government sets limits on how much of these substances can be released, and exceeding those limits is illegal.
real_world_examples: A textile dyeing unit in Surat discharging untreated effluents containing heavy metals like chromium and lead into the Tapi river, exceeding prescribed concentration limits under the Environment Protection Act.
A thermal power plant in Jharkhand emitting fly ash and sulphur dioxide beyond the permissible emission standards set by the Central Government, thereby polluting the surrounding air and soil.
A chemical manufacturing company in Ankleshwar GIDC releasing toxic volatile organic compounds (VOCs) into the atmosphere, which qualify as gaseous environmental pollutants under the Act.

A stone-crushing unit near Faridabad generating particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10) in concentrations far exceeding the prescribed air quality standards, constituting environmental pollutants under Section 7.

A paper mill in Uttarakhand discharging chlorine-based compounds and dissolved solids into a local river system, where the concentration of these substances is injurious to aquatic life and downstream communities.

Excessive noise from a fireworks manufacturing unit in Sivakasi exceeding the prescribed decibel limits, constituting noise as an environmental pollutant under the maximum allowable limits specified in rules framed under Section 6.
what_it_covers: Gaseous emissions such as sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and carbon monoxide released from factory chimneys or industrial combustion processes in excess of prescribed standards.

Liquid effluents discharged from industries into water bodies, including heavy metals, dissolved chemicals, and biological oxygen demand (BOD)-heavy wastewater exceeding allowable concentration limits.
Solid or semi-solid waste substances, including fly ash, industrial sludge, or chemical residues, whose presence in soil or water at certain concentrations is injurious to the environment.
Noise pollution generated by industrial machinery, operations, or processes that exceeds the maximum permissible decibel levels prescribed for different areas under Section 6.
Hazardous chemical substances discharged or emitted from manufacturing, processing, or handling operations that may tend to be injurious to environment or human health.
what_it_excludes: Natural background levels of substances in the environment that do not exceed prescribed concentration thresholds and are not injurious or tending to be injurious to the environment.
Substances discharged or emitted within the permissible limits prescribed by the Central Government under Section 7, which are lawfully regulated and do not constitute a violation under the Act.
Agricultural runoff or naturally occurring geological leaching of minerals into water bodies that is not attributable to any industry, operation, or process covered under the Act.

Substances that are hazardous in nature but are being lawfully handled, stored, or transported strictly in accordance with prescribed safeguards and procedures, and not yet discharged or emitted into the environment.
Purely biological or organic matter decomposing naturally in a controlled and lawful manner that does not reach injurious concentration levels in the surrounding environment.
definitions.why_it_matters: Whether a substance qualifies as an environmental pollutant directly determines the applicability of the prohibition under Section 7, which makes it unlawful for any person carrying on industry, operation, or process to discharge or emit it in excess of prescribed standards, thereby triggering criminal liability including imprisonment and fines under the Act. It also activates the Central Government's powers under Sections 3, 6, and 25 to lay down standards, conduct inspections, and issue directions, making this definition the foundational trigger for virtually all enforcement and regulatory action under the Environment Protection Act.

definitions.plain_english: Environmental pollution refers to a situation where any harmful solid, liquid, or gaseous substance is present in the surroundings — including water, air, and land — at levels that are or could be damaging. Essentially, it is what happens when a pollutant enters and exists within our natural environment. It covers any such presence, regardless of how it got there or whether harm has already occurred.
real_world_examples: A textile dyeing unit in Surat discharging untreated effluents containing toxic chemicals into the Tapi River, causing the concentration of harmful substances in the water to reach injurious levels — constituting environmental pollution of a water body.

A thermal power plant in Jharkhand emitting fly ash and sulphur dioxide beyond permissible limits into the atmosphere, resulting in the presence of these pollutants in the surrounding air at concentrations harmful to residents and vegetation.

Illegal dumping of industrial solid waste containing heavy metals such as lead and cadmium by a battery manufacturing unit near Pune on open land, leading to the presence of toxic substances in the soil and groundwater.

Oil spills from a refinery in Vadinar, Gujarat, releasing petroleum hydrocarbons into the coastal marine environment, causing the presence of hazardous liquid pollutants in seawater and affecting marine ecosystems.

Burning of crop stubble in Punjab and Haryana releasing particulate matter (PM2.5) and carbon monoxide into the air, creating a condition of environmental pollution that severely affects air quality in Delhi-NCR during winter months.
what_it_covers: Presence of toxic industrial effluents in a river at concentrations injurious to aquatic life and human health.
Presence of gaseous emissions such as sulphur dioxide or nitrogen oxides in the air surrounding a factory at harmful concentration levels.
Presence of hazardous solid waste leachate in soil or groundwater resulting from improper disposal of industrial by-products.
Presence of noise beyond permissible limits in a residential zone caused by industrial operations, as noise is recognised as an environmental pollutant under related rules.
Presence of pesticide residues in agricultural land water runoff at concentrations injurious to micro-organisms, plants, or human beings.
what_it_excludes: Mere handling, storage, or transport of a pollutant substance that has not yet entered or been released into the environment, as the definition requires actual presence in the environment.

Substances present in the environment at concentrations that are not injurious and do not tend to be injurious — i.e., below harmful threshold levels — since the definition of 'environmental pollutant' itself requires injurious concentration.
Natural background levels of substances such as naturally occurring minerals or gases present in soil or water that do not meet the threshold of being injurious to the environment.
Pollution occurring exclusively within a closed industrial system or contained manufacturing process where no substance has been released into the external environment (water, air, or land).

Social or economic harm caused by industrial activity that does not involve the presence of a pollutant substance in the environment, such as noise from traffic that does not reach injurious concentrations under prescribed standards.

definitions.definition: An act or intended act is deemed to be done in 'good faith' under this Act when it is performed honestly and without malice or fraudulent intent in pursuance of the Environment Protection Act, 1986, or the rules, orders, or directions issued thereunder, regardless of whether the act is done with or without negligence.
definitions.plain_english: Good faith means that a government officer or authority member acted honestly and sincerely while carrying out their duties under the Environment Protection Act, without any dishonest or malicious motive. If someone genuinely believed they were doing the right thing under the law, they are protected even if the action later turns out to be wrong. This protection applies as long as the person was genuinely trying to follow the law and not acting corruptly or deceitfully.
real_world_examples: A Central Pollution Control Board inspector in Maharashtra issues a closure direction to a factory believing it is violating emission standards based on available test data, but the factory later proves the data was erroneous — the inspector is protected from any lawsuit because they acted in good faith on the information available.

An officer of the State Environment Department in Gujarat issues an order restricting the discharge of effluents into a river based on a Government Analyst's report, and the factory owner files a case claiming wrongful loss of business — the officer cannot be prosecuted because the action was taken honestly in pursuance of the Act.

A designated authority member in Tamil Nadu enters and inspects a chemical plant premises under Section 10 of the Act, suspecting hazardous substance leakage, but the inspection later reveals no violation — no legal proceedings can be brought against the authority member since the entry was made in good faith.

An authorised officer in Uttar Pradesh directs the collection of samples from an industrial unit near the Ganga under the Act's provisions based on a public complaint, and the unit sues for harassment — the suit is barred because the officer acted in good faith in pursuance of the Act's mandate.

A senior Environment Protection officer in Himachal Pradesh issues an emergency order halting a construction project near a protected forest area on the basis of an incomplete environmental impact report, and the developer seeks damages — the officer is shielded from liability as the action was intended to be done in good faith under the Act.

Orders, directions, or decisions issued by any authority constituted under the Act when such actions are taken sincerely and without corrupt or dishonest intent, in pursuance of the Act or rules made thereunder.

Members, officers, or employees of pollution control boards or other constituted authorities who conduct inspections, collect samples, or issue notices, provided their actions are intended to implement the Act honestly.
Intended but not yet completed actions — i.e., actions that are in the process of being taken in pursuance of the Act — are also protected under the good faith clause.
what_it_excludes: Actions taken by government officers or authority members with malicious intent, personal vendetta, or corrupt motive — such acts do not qualify as good faith and are not protected under Section 18.

Acts by private individuals, companies, or occupiers who are not officers or employees of the Government or constituted authorities — good faith protection under Section 18 is exclusively available to government and authority personnel.

Actions that are taken completely outside the scope of the Environment Protection Act, its rules, or any orders and directions issued thereunder — unauthorized or wholly extraneous acts cannot be shielded by the good faith provision.

Actions where gross negligence or willful disregard for established procedure is established against an officer, as such conduct may negate the honest intent required for the good faith shield to apply.
definitions.why_it_matters: The good faith provision under Section 18 is a complete bar to any suit, prosecution, or other legal proceeding against the Government or its officers and authority members acting under the Act, ensuring that enforcement personnel can discharge their duties without fear of personal legal liability. If this definition applies, no civil, criminal, or other proceedings can be initiated against such persons, enabling robust and fearless implementation of environmental protection measures.

definitions.definition: "Hazardous substance" means any substance or preparation which, by reason of its chemical or physico-chemical properties or handling, is liable to cause harm to human beings, other living creatures, plant, micro-organism, property or the environment.
definitions.plain_english: A hazardous substance is any material or mixture of materials that can cause harm to people, animals, plants, tiny organisms, property, or the environment, either because of its chemical nature or because of the way it is handled. This includes substances that are dangerous on their own as well as those that become dangerous when they are manufactured, stored, transported, or used. Even a substance that is not inherently dangerous can qualify if its handling makes it liable to cause harm.
real_world_examples: Bhopal Gas Tragedy context: Methyl isocyanate (MIC) stored at the Union Carbide plant in Bhopal qualifies as a hazardous substance because its physico-chemical properties made it capable of causing mass harm to human beings and other living creatures upon accidental release.

A chlorine gas cylinder used in water treatment plants across Indian municipal corporations is a hazardous substance, as chlorine's chemical properties pose serious risk of harm to humans, animals, and vegetation if leaked during storage or transportation.

Mercury-containing waste generated by chlor-alkali factories along the Periyar river in Kerala constitutes a hazardous substance, as its physico-chemical properties make it liable to contaminate water bodies and harm aquatic life, micro-organisms, and human populations downstream.

Endosulfan pesticide, widely used in cashew plantations in Kasaragod district, Kerala, is a hazardous substance because its chemical properties caused documented harm to human beings, other living creatures, and the surrounding environment over decades of aerial spraying.

Hydrofluoric acid used in semiconductor manufacturing units in Bengaluru's electronics industrial zones is a hazardous substance, as both its inherent chemical corrosiveness and the manner of its handling in industrial processes make it liable to cause serious harm to workers and the environment.

Fly ash generated by coal-fired thermal power stations such as those operated by NTPC in Singrauli, Madhya Pradesh, can qualify as a hazardous substance when its handling (uncontrolled dumping near water bodies) makes it liable to harm soil, water, micro-organisms, and nearby communities.

Preparations (mixtures or formulations) of multiple chemicals that collectively exhibit hazardous physico-chemical properties, even if individual components may not separately meet the threshold of harm.

They can escape punishment only by proving they did not know about the violation or that they took all reasonable steps to prevent it.

definitions.definition: Neglect, as used in Section 17 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, refers to the failure of an officer of a Government Department to exercise reasonable care, attention, or duty in preventing the commission of an offence under this Act, where such failure is attributable to the officer and the offence is proved to have resulted from that omission. It denotes a culpable omission of duty rather than an intentional act.
definitions.plain_english: Neglect means that a government officer failed to do something they were supposed to do — like monitor, supervise, or take action — and because of that failure, an environmental offence occurred. It is not about deliberately causing harm, but about not being careful or diligent enough in carrying out official responsibilities. If an officer's carelessness allowed pollution or an environmental violation to happen, that counts as neglect under this law.
real_world_examples: A Deputy Secretary in the Ministry of Environment fails to inspect or review reports of illegal chemical discharge from a government-owned factory into the Yamuna river, resulting in a major water pollution incident — the officer's inaction constitutes neglect under Section 17.

An officer in a State Public Works Department is responsible for overseeing construction waste disposal but repeatedly ignores internal complaints about hazardous debris being dumped near a residential area, leading to soil contamination — this omission qualifies as neglect.

A senior engineer in a government-run thermal power plant fails to ensure the functioning of pollution control equipment despite being aware of its breakdown, resulting in excess fly ash emission beyond prescribed standards — such failure to act is neglect.

An official in a Municipal Corporation's sanitation department neglects to enforce wastewater treatment protocols at a government sewage plant, causing untreated effluent to flow into a local lake, triggering environmental harm attributable to the officer's neglect.

A forest department officer fails to act on documented reports of encroachment and burning of protected forest land by subordinates under their charge, allowing environmental damage to continue — the officer's inaction constitutes neglect under the Act.

A government official's omission to implement or enforce prescribed environmental safeguards within their department, resulting in pollution or hazardous substance mishandling.

Offences committed entirely without any involvement, knowledge, or supervisory connection to the officer concerned, where the causal link to neglect cannot be established.
Private company officers or directors, whose liability for neglect is governed separately under Section 16 and not Section 17.
Negligence by non-officer employees or subordinate staff who do not hold official duty or charge over the relevant environmental function.

An entrepreneur running a small-scale electroplating unit in Ludhiana, Punjab, who personally oversees the handling of heavy metal solutions and controls the affairs of the unit, is the 'occupier' liable under the Act.

A port trust authority in Mumbai that holds custody of imported hazardous chemicals stored in its bonded warehouse would be considered the 'occupier' in relation to those substances while they remain in its possession.

definitions.definition: "Prescribed" means prescribed by rules made under this Act.
definitions.plain_english: "Prescribed" refers to anything that is specifically set out or determined by the official rules created under the Environment Protection Act. When the Act says something must be done in a "prescribed" manner or within "prescribed" limits, it means the details are found in the rules that the Central Government has formally written and notified. This allows the Act to set broad obligations while leaving specific technical details to be filled in through subordinate legislation.
real_world_examples: Under Section 8, a factory in Gujarat handling chlorine gas must follow the exact handling procedures and safety safeguards prescribed in the Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989, made under this Act — those rules are what 'prescribed' refers to in that context.

A chemical plant in Maharashtra discharging treated effluents into a river must ensure concentrations of pollutants do not exceed the limits prescribed in the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, which specify permissible standards for various industries.

Under Section 11, Central Government inspectors exercising powers of entry and inspection must carry out their functions in the manner prescribed by rules — for instance, following specified notice requirements or documentation procedures outlined in the subordinate rules.

A pesticide manufacturing unit in Punjab storing hazardous substances must comply with packaging and labelling safeguards as prescribed under the relevant rules notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, not just general industry practices.

When a petrochemical company in Andhra Pradesh seeks to know the permissible noise emission levels for its operations, it refers to the standards 'prescribed' in the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986, schedules of which list environment-specific standards enforceable under the Act.
what_it_covers: Standards, limits, and thresholds for environmental pollutants set out in rules notified by the Central Government under this Act, such as emission concentration limits.
Procedures and safeguards for handling hazardous substances as detailed in rules framed under this Act, applicable under Section 8.
Authorities, agencies, forms, fees, and procedural requirements specified in rules made under this Act that govern how obligations in the main provisions are to be discharged.
Any technical specification, schedule, or guideline formally incorporated into rules under this Act and thereby given the force of law.
what_it_excludes: Guidelines, circulars, or advisories issued by Government departments or agencies that are not formally enacted as rules under this Act — these are not 'prescribed' within the meaning of the term.

Standards or procedures set by other statutes such as the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 or the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 — those are not 'prescribed' under this Act.
Internal company policies, industry self-regulatory codes, or ISO standards adopted voluntarily, even if environmentally relevant, since they are not made under this Act.
Orders, directions, or notifications issued under Section 5 of this Act that are not framed as 'rules' under the rule-making power — these fall outside the specific meaning of 'prescribed.'

definitions.plain_english: Prescribed authorities are the government bodies or agencies officially designated under the Environment Protection Act to receive emergency notifications when a harmful pollution event occurs or is about to occur. These are the official entities that coordinate the response to environmental accidents and order cleanup and remedial actions. They are identified through official government rules and notifications, not within the Act itself.
real_world_examples: A chemical factory in Ankleshwar, Gujarat accidentally releases toxic effluent into the Amlakhadi river — the factory manager must immediately notify the prescribed authority, such as the Gujarat Pollution Control Board, and render all assistance demanded.

An oil tanker spill occurs in Mumbai Harbour threatening coastal ecosystems — the shipping company must intimate the prescribed authority (such as the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board or Coast Guard as designated) and assist in containment operations.

A pesticide manufacturing unit in Bhopal suffers a pipeline rupture causing gas leakage — the person in charge must forthwith inform the prescribed authority under the Environment Protection Rules and comply with all remedial directions issued.

A mining company in Jharkhand discharges acid mine drainage beyond prescribed standards into a nearby stream due to a dam failure — the prescribed authority (Central Pollution Control Board or State Pollution Control Board as notified) must be immediately intimated and the company must render full assistance for remediation.

An industrial estate in Pune has a fire leading to release of hazardous chemical smoke — the occupier must notify the prescribed authority designated under Environment Protection Rules and assist in air quality monitoring and evacuation coordination as directed.
what_it_covers: State Pollution Control Boards designated under Environment Protection Rules as prescribed authorities to receive accident notifications and coordinate remedial action.
The Central Pollution Control Board when notified as a prescribed authority for receiving intimation of environmental pollution incidents of national significance.
Any other agency or government body specifically identified through rules made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 to respond to environmental emergencies.
District-level or regional environmental regulatory officers who may be prescribed to receive on-ground intimation and direct immediate remedial operations.
what_it_excludes: Private environmental consultancy firms or NGOs, regardless of their role in environmental management, as they are not government-prescribed statutory authorities.

Municipal corporations or local bodies acting in their general civic capacity, unless they have been specifically notified as prescribed authorities under the rules.

definitions.definition: Prescribed standards means the standards for discharge or emission of environmental pollutants as may be prescribed by the Central Government by rules made under this Act, in excess of which no person carrying on any industry, operation or process shall discharge or emit or permit to be discharged or emitted any environmental pollutant, and in excess of which any discharge occurring or apprehended to occur due to accident or other unforeseen act or event triggers mandatory reporting and mitigation obligations.
definitions.plain_english: Prescribed standards are the legally fixed limits set by the Central Government that determine how much pollution — such as smoke, chemicals, or wastewater — a factory or industry is allowed to release into the environment. real_world_examples: A textile dyeing unit in Surat discharges treated effluent into the Tapi river. The Central Government has prescribed a maximum permissible limit of 250 mg/litre of Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) for such discharge. If the unit's effluent exceeds this limit, it violates Section 7 of the Environment Protection Act.

A thermal power plant in Jharkhand emits particulate matter from its chimney stacks. The prescribed standard for particulate matter emission for coal-based power plants is set by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. Any emission beyond this prescribed limit exposes the plant to prosecution and closure orders.

A chemical factory in Ankleshwar, Gujarat suffers a sudden tank rupture and accidental discharge of toxic effluent into a nearby stream in quantities exceeding the prescribed standards. Under Section 9, the factory owner is immediately obligated to notify the prescribed authorities and assist in remediation, failing which they are liable for recovery of remediation expenses.

A tannery cluster in Kanpur is found discharging chromium-laden wastewater into the Ganga at concentrations exceeding the prescribed standards for heavy metals. The Central Pollution Control Board directs closure of non-compliant units and initiates recovery of clean-up costs from the tannery owners as arrears of land revenue.

A brick kiln in Punjab emits smoke containing sulphur dioxide beyond the prescribed ambient air quality standards. An authorised officer collects samples and the Government Analyst confirms the excess. The kiln owner faces penalties under the Environment Protection Act for violating the prescribed standards under Section 7.

definitions.plain_english: Any member, officer, or employee of the environmental authority set up under this Act is treated as a government public servant while doing their official duties under this law. This means they get the same legal protections and are subject to the same responsibilities as any other government official. If someone bribes or obstructs them, or if they misuse their position, the relevant IPC provisions on public servants apply.
real_world_examples: An inspector appointed by the Central Pollution Control Board under section 3 authority who visits a factory in Ludhiana to check effluent discharge levels is acting as a public servant — obstructing or bribing him constitutes an offence under IPC sections on public servants.

A member of an environment authority board constituted under section 3 who approves or denies environmental clearance for a thermal power plant in Jharkhand is acting as a public servant; any gratification offered to influence the decision amounts to bribery under IPC.

An employee of an authority constituted under section 3 who collects water samples from the Yamuna river for testing under this Act is performing duties as a public servant — assaulting or threatening him during this act is an offence under IPC provisions applicable to public servants.
